subject: Copula on observed variable and latent variable

messages.author: 3268b1ddfb2eb06a
messages.subject: Copula on observed variable and latent variable
parts:
Consider observed data y1 and y2. y1 is measured on a continuous scale and y2 is measured on a binary scale. A latent variable z is assumed to generate y2 as: y2 = I(z > 0). Furthermore, a copula model dependency between y1 and z. This model could be written hierarchically (with some abuse of notation) as:

y2        =  I(z > 0)
(y1, z)  ~  C(F_y1( |w), F_z( |w) | phi)
w, phi   ~ priors

where w is the vector of marginal parameters for y1 and z, F_y1 and F_z are respective marginal cdfs for y1 and z, phi is the copula parameter.

How could this be modelled in Stan? I have written a custom probability function to sample y1 and z from the bivariate likelihood produced by the copula. What I don't know how to do is to account for (generate?) the latent variable(s) z, and how to specify the relationship between y2 and z.

Thank you,
Ved Deshpande

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Copula on observed variable and latent variable
parts:
Dear Ved,

you could model y2 as binary logit or as step {0,1} probability. I'm not aware, how the discontinuity is handled by STAN.
It mostly leads, in optimization, to NP-hard optimization problems.
Thus for the first y2 could be:

y2 <- inv_logit(z)
z ~ normal(0,5); 

If you model y2 as a step function your distribution becomes a PMF in which you need to take the differences in C.

Andre

Andre- Thank you for your suggestions. One thing to note is that the latent variable z is continuous- so the copula is on two continuous variables.

z and y1 have to be sampled together, using the bivariate likelihood that the copula provides. I can do this in Stan. So let's assume I can get (with abuse of notation):

(y1, z) ~ F where F is a bivariate probability distribution.

Since I need y2 to be a binary variable, I think

y2 <- inv_logit(z)

would not be appropriate. That would mean that y2 is a probability. y2 ~ bernoulli(Inv_logit(z)) is also inappropriate because z does not play the role of the linear predictor function here.

I don't think I can do away with z, since it is part of the copula. So I might be forced to use the step function. Could you please provide some more clarification on what I need to do regarding:
"If you model y2 as a step function your distribution becomes a PMF in which you need to take the differences in C."

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Copula on observed variable and latent variable
parts:
Ved,

(y1,z) should considered to be independent. They are used to define the marginal CDF as input to the Copula. 
Lets call this copula C. 

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(probability_theory)

Have a look at Definition: 

In probabilistic terms,  is a d-dimensional copula if C is a joint cumulative distribution function of a d-dimensional random vector on the unit cube  with uniform marginals.[1]

That means, we have to map (y1,z) to [0,1]^2  in our case. 

We decided already to map y2 via y2 <- inv_logit(z) which maps z to [0,1],
next we have to map y1 to [0,1]. 
Thus we need to assume a marginal distribution to y1. 

As example, we could  sample y1 as  
y1 ~ normal(0,1)
and then we would need a STAN function to calculate the cdf of the
univariate standard normal distribution. Thus y1_cdf <- normal_cdf(y1,0,1);

Or directly sample to y1_cdf ~ uniform(0,1); 

And lets assume C is a frank copula:
 

then u: = y1_cdf and v :=  y2 and 
theta ~ normal(0,5); 
(If rare case theta == 0, the term becomes NAN and being rejected by 
the sampler)
the frank copula above defines a CDF.
For log-likelihood estimation in STAN we need the density c(u,v,theta) of 
our copula C(u,v,theta). Wikipedia doesn't provide them, but
you can easily take the derivatives or search the internet. 

Last step would be to add
increment_log_prob(log(c(u,v,theta)));

In the discrete case, we cannot take the
derivatives, we have to take the differences.
This result into a copula probability mass function,
which can be found here, eg. 

http://www-1.ms.ut.ee/tartu07/presentations/kolev.pdf

Visualise the probability mass function as one or more
plateau(s) or hyperplanes connected together. 

Andre
